title: debugging production incidents and root cause analysis
concepts: An incident is an unplanned interruption or degradation of a service that needs coordinated response. Declare it early when user impact is plausible; investigation and severity can be refined as evidence arrives.

Incident command separates coordination from hands-on diagnosis. Clear roles, a shared timeline, an incident channel, and regular updates reduce duplicated work and let responders focus on mitigation.

Restore user-facing service first. Mitigation can include rollback, traffic shifting, feature disablement, capacity protection, or graceful degradation; a permanent code fix can follow after risk is understood.
Troubleshooting forms and tests hypotheses using observable evidence. Change one variable at a time when possible, preserve logs and timestamps, and distinguish correlation from causal explanation.

A postmortem records impact, timeline, contributing conditions, recovery, and specific preventive actions. Blameless analysis examines the system and incentives that shaped decisions rather than searching for one person to blame.
Follow-up work needs an owner, priority, and completion evidence. Repeated incidents are a signal that prior actions did not remove the failure mechanism or were not implemented.

scopeExclusions: The incident command system, on-call rotations, alert design, security/governance, operational playbooks, and detailed restoration options are covered in t09-012. This senior-interview topic applies incident reasoning to technical diagnosis, response narrative, causal analysis, and interview scenarios; do not reproduce the full operations reference.
Specific production diagnostic commands and profiler tools are covered in t09-013; this topic uses observable evidence generically and does not duplicate that tooling reference.
Tool-specific incident management automation and Azure SRE Agent integration belong to infrastructure operations.
Routine application debugging and .NET profiling belong to t09-013.
Reliability design patterns and service-level objectives are covered in architecture and operations topics.
Detailed organization-wide crisis communications, legal disclosure, and regulatory reporting vary by employer and jurisdiction.
Incident response focuses on service reliability, not security breach forensics or law-enforcement procedures.
accuracyFacts: Google SRE's incident-command role model uses an incident commander, operations lead, and communications lead as one documented pattern. Organizations adapt role names and assignments; severity scales, declaration thresholds, and response procedures are local policy rather than universal standards.

During a major outage, prioritize limiting user harm and restoring service while preserving evidence for later diagnosis. Root-cause investigation should not delay a safe mitigation when service or data is at risk.

A useful troubleshooting test should distinguish competing hypotheses while accounting for its own side effects and confounding conditions. Record the expected behavior, observed behavior, reproduction conditions, test performed, and result.

Postmortems should describe impact, actions, contributing causes, and follow-up work without indicting individuals. Systems thinking examines the information, tools, incentives, and constraints that made actions locally reasonable.

A single 'root cause' label can oversimplify a complex incident. Explain triggers, contributing factors, detection/response conditions, and defenses; use causal language only where evidence supports it.
Recovery is verified through user-facing service indicators and critical workflows, not inferred solely from a successful deploy or a quiet alert stream.
Time-to-detect, acknowledge, mitigate, and restore metrics require consistent event definitions and start/stop points; organization-specific incident policies may define them differently.
